source.title: Scale Can't Overcome Pragmatics: The Impact of Reporting Bias on Vision-Language Reasoning
source.authors: Amita Kamath; Jack Hessel; K. Chandu; Jena D. Hwang; Kai-Wei Chang; Ranjay Krishna

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present, with minor text-extraction formatting artifacts.
record.tranche_reason: The paper's own scaling sweeps on vision-language reasoning benchmarks argue that scaling does not reliably improve these downstream behaviors; it reports a different modality and measure from the original language-model pretraining-loss studies.
record.gate_note: The paper tests OpenCLIP scaling on four reasoning benchmarks and reports comparisons across model scales. It also reports LLaVA-1.5 scores at 7B and 13B. Results cited from other papers, such as prior scaling findings on ImageNet, are not recorded as rows. The study does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations.
record.test_reason: Section 5.3 fits scaling curves for 32 OpenCLIP models (LAION-80M/400M/2B; 3B/13B/34B samples seen) on four reasoning benchmarks. It also compares LLaVA-1.5 7B vs 13B. These are the study's own results on whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale (V6), and the authors argue scaling fails for most of these skills. The measure is downstream benchmark error, not pretraining loss, so V1–V4 and V7 are not tested. V5 is treated as untested because the rows measure downstream task error, not the pretraining-loss power law.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that reporting bias in image-text data under-represents spatial, temporal, negation and counting reasoning, and that scaling data or model size (or adding multilingual data) does not make these skills emerge. Reasoning-aware annotator instructions help, shown by a counting fine-tuning gain. They caveat that scaling laws could fail at much higher scales.
record.recipe_differences: Uses vision-language models and reasoning-benchmark performance/loss across model and data scales, rather than language-model held-out pretraining cross-entropy. It does not fit small-run loss to predict larger runs or identify compute-optimal parameter/token splits.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies by benchmark: counting improves with compute, negation only slightly, and spatial and temporal reasoning show no stated compute-related improvement. The multilingual-data model underperforms the English-caption CLIP ViT-B/32 reference on all four Table 2 benchmarks.
record.peer_reviewed: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The scaling results concern reasoning-benchmark behavior rather than held-out pretraining loss. The authors note that scaling-law extrapolations might fail at much higher scales. Figure 3 is not accompanied by uncertainty estimates in the text, and the 32-model sweep is reported in aggregate.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 scores for non-scaling comparison models, including Molmo and closed-source models, were left out because the paper does not present them as a model- or data-scale sweep. The qualitative statement that closed-data models perform well is likewise not a scale comparison.

untested.parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolating small-run loss fits to much larger runs. The authors extrapolate downstream error to human level but never check a prediction against a larger run.
Effects of depth, width or architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
Power-law form of pretraining (contrastive) loss for vision-language models. Only downstream benchmark error is fitted; the ImageNet curve is cited from Cherti et al.
Sensitivity of exponents or compute-optimal split to fitting or setup choices.

missing.what: Disentangled model-scale vs data-scale analysis, stated to show equivalent trends to the compute curves; no numbers given.
Fitted scaling-law parameters or error values per model in Figure 3 (log-log fits), needed for comparing rates across studies; only qualitative text is recorded.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. Table 2(a) single-model rows (r5, r7–r11, r13–r17, r19–r23, r25–r28) stay cannot_determine as isolated points. Read as a size series, they show no clear upward trend for spatial (30.6→26.0), negation or temporal, and a rise then plateau for counting (43.4→64.1→60.0). The training-data scale behind each Table 2 model is not stated. The LLaVA comparison has only two sizes, so it bears on whether performance improves with scale, not on its predictability. The record's V5 labels were dropped because downstream benchmark error is a V6 measure.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs' held-out pretraining loss from fits on smaller runs.
The loss-minimizing parameter/token allocation at fixed compute, including its exponents.
Effects of architecture depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.

The study tests scaling behavior for vision-language models on reasoning benchmarks, not held-out pretraining loss; it does not test image generation, video, repeated data, or fine-tuning and transfer scaling laws.
Downstream benchmark performance is evaluated against model and data scale, but the study does not test prediction from pretraining loss.
The study does not test how fitting choices, parameter counting, or training schedules change exponents or compute-optimal allocations.
